opening.headline: The problem of the same assistant giving different answers to different people is solved by dividing rules to be written in instructions and requests to be spoken in conversations.
body: It is common for AI assistants used by a team to answer in a different tone and format for each person. In many cases, it is not because the assistant has changed, but because each person has a different request at the beginning of the conversation.

In this lesson, we distinguish between system-level instructions, which are written down once in the assistant settings, and during-conversation instructions, which are entered on the fly in a chat window. Check where guidelines are placed in the ChatGPT project, GPT, Claude project, and Gemini's Gem, and learn the standards for determining which rules should be placed where.

objectives: Differences between system-level instructions and interactive instructions can be explained in terms of persistence and coverage.
Can distinguish between rules to put in instructions and instructions to say each time

screens.title: It's the same assistant, but each person answers differently.

visual.alt: A scene where three people's different response speech bubbles are placed side by side under one situation card.
labels: Same question: Please summarize the results of Company A’s meeting this quarter.

paragraphs: We have a report assistant that our sales team uses together. Ga-eun received an answer written in formal language, Do-yoon received a summary in casual language, and Seo-yeon received an answer mixed in English. Three people asked the same question, but the writing style, length, and use of tables were all different.

The cause was not that the assistant had changed. Each person had a different request at the beginning of the conversation. There was a mix of people who wrote down rules in the chat window every time and people who did not.
There is only one question in this class. Which rules should you write down once, and which should you say every time?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: It is difficult to achieve results by remembering and entering the rules for each person. We need to decide where the rules will stay.

screens.outro: Let’s start by recalling your own experience.

screens.title: Have you ever repeated your business rules in every conversation?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Every time you ask for a report, have you ever written it down again, “in formal language, without tables, in three lines?”
items.answer: Many people have this experience. If you are writing down the same sentence over and over again, that sentence is not something you do today, but something you must always do. Sentences like these are candidates for guidelines.

items.prompt: Have you ever explained again the tone you decided on yesterday in a new conversation today?
items.answer: Conversations start anew each time you open them, so anything you said in yesterday's chat window won't automatically be followed into the new conversation. Rules that must be maintained in new conversations should be written in the Assistant settings, not in the conversation window.

items.prompt: Is the sentence you write down repeatedly “what I do today” or “what I should always do”?
items.answer: The two are often mixed. “Today, please write a review of Company A’s meeting” is today’s request, and “Write in a respectful manner” is a rule that will always be followed. This class covers the criteria for distinguishing between the two types.

screens.outro: Now that you have a sense that there is a separate sentence that is repeated, I will introduce the place where the sentence stays.

screens.title: System-level and in-conversational instructions: Persistence and scope of coverage.
screens.lead: Use the switch below to switch between states with and without instructions. You can see how the answers to the same question vary.

visual.alt: Structural diagram with a line running from the instruction box on the left to the three dialogs on the right.

states.label: Instructions available
states.body: System-level guidelines are rules that you write down once in your Assistant settings. It automatically applies to all conversations with that assistant, so when three people ask the same question, they get the answer in the same style and format. This property is called persistence. The scope of coverage is an entire project or GPT. ChatGPT project guidelines apply only within that project and take precedence over global custom guidelines. According to the Claude Project Guide, a project's guidelines are used for all chats in that project.

states.label: no instructions
states.body: Without instructions, the rules rely only on instructions during the conversation. In-conversation instructions are requests entered in a chat window and are effective only within that conversation. Coverage is one conversation. When you open a new conversation, you have to write it again, and if each person writes differently, the response will also be different. The Claude Project instructions explain that context is not automatically shared between chats within a project, so what you say in one chat won't carry over to another. If instructions are the foundation of every conversation, instructions during conversations are the call of the day.

screens.outro: Now that we've defined the concept, let's check where this spot is on the screen for the three companies' products.

screens.title: Location of Project·GPT·Gem instructions
screens.lead: Select each tab to find a place to write instructions for the three companies' products. Note that although the names are different, the structures are similar.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: In the ChatGPT project, open the more (•••) in the project menu, select Project settings, and write down the project instructions. Example tips include “Act like a marketing mentor, write concisely, use bullet points, and ask questions back.” In the Instructions section of the GPT builder, write down the behavioral rules for the entire GPT. GPT Help describes the guidelines as something that applies to all conversations, guiding tone, structure, and judgment. The project also has a separate place to upload files, so rules and data are separated.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: On the Claude project screen, select Set project instructions, write down how you want the assistant to behave and respond, and click Save instructions to save them. These guidelines will be used in all chats for that project. There is a separate project knowledge area on the right side of the screen where you can upload documents, text files, or code snippets. Context is not automatically shared between chats, so you should always include the necessary information in instructions or project knowledge.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body: In Gemini, you create a new Gem from Gems in the sidebar, giving it a name and instructions. You must check the operation with the preview on the right and click Save to save it. Gem Help tells you to think about four areas when writing instructions: persona, task, context, and format. The section for uploading files to be used as knowledge is also separate from the instructions section.

tabs.label: common structure
tabs.body: All three products have separate sections for writing instructions and posting information. Instructions determine how to act, and knowledge determines what to refer to. What you write in the instructions box will apply to all conversations using that project, GPT, or Gem. Therefore, the question is the same for any product. Are these rules necessary for every conversation?

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the location, let's look at the criteria for deciding what to put in the guidelines and what to leave in the conversation.

screens.title: Criteria for deciding what to include in guidelines and what to leave in conversation
screens.lead: When you select the highlighted phrase in the example sentences below, an explanation will appear indicating which of the three criteria it meets. Click on the verses one by one.

data.text:
[Requests accumulated in Report Assistant]
- All reports are written with courtesy.
- The results are summarized in three lines.
- Don't guess what you don't know, but ask questions.
- Today, please summarize the review of Company A’s meeting.
- Please adjust the amount to be reported by this Friday.
- Please write it in one page only this time.

marks.span: All reports are written with courtesy.
marks.note: Meets Criterion 1 repeatability and Criterion 2 range. It's a candidate for guidance because you end up saying the same thing every time and it applies to every conversation. In your instructions, write these sentences in one short, clear line.

marks.span: The results are summarized in three lines.
marks.note: Corresponds to criterion 3 stability. These are formatting rules that won't change for months, so it makes sense to write them down once in the instructions.

marks.span: Don't guess what you don't know, but ask questions.
marks.note: Since it is a principle of action, it is the same in any conversation about any topic. Since the scope is all conversation, it goes into the instructions.

marks.span: Today, please summarize the review of Company A’s meeting.
marks.note: This topic is specific to what we are doing today. If I write it down in the instructions, I'll leave it in the conversation because I'll end up making the mistake of trying to answer the same topic in tomorrow's conversation.

marks.span: Please adjust the amount to be reported by this Friday.
marks.note: This is a condition for the date to change. It is less reliable, so leave it as an instruction during the conversation. Most sentences containing dates or deadlines are of this type.

marks.span: Please write it in one page only this time.
marks.note: This is a quantity requirement that is only needed once. These are instructions during a conversation, as they are not repeated. Inserting a condition that is only required once into the instructions has the side effect of locking all subsequent responses into one page.

screens.outro: Now that we have the criteria in place, let's take a look at how an instructor directly classifies a case.

screens.title: Explanation: Classify the twelve lines of the Report Assistant's rules.
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to follow the instructor as he breaks down the rules one by one. Pay attention to the reasons for each judgment.

visual.alt: A classification diagram in which the twelve lines of rules on the left are divided into two boxes on the right.
labels: Today, please summarize the review of Company A’s meeting.

steps.title: Check the situation
steps.body: There are a dozen rows of notes left by team members in the Sales Report Assistant. They're all mixed up in one place, so it's hard to tell which are the rules you'll always follow and which are the requests of the day. The instructor categorizes the items one by one based on three criteria: repeatability, range, and stability.

steps.title: “Write with respect.”
steps.body: This is a sentence that is written every time, applies to all reports, and does not change for a long time. Since all three criteria are met, we move towards the guidelines.

steps.title: “Today, summarize the review of Company A’s meeting.”
steps.body: This is today's topic. Tomorrow we will be talking about another company, so it would be difficult to leave it as a guideline. Leave it as an instruction during the conversation.

steps.title: “No tickets are used”
steps.body: These are formal rules that are repeated and unchanging in every conversation. Move to instructions.

steps.title: “Report by this Friday”
steps.body: Dates change weekly. If you write it down in the instructions, the same deadline will follow next week, so leave it as an instruction during the conversation.

steps.title: Classification results
steps.body: Of the twelve lines, five lines remain on the instructions side and seven lines remain on the dialogue side. The instructions are now one short page, and team members don't have to write down the text every time, just say the request of the day. When the rules are gathered in one place, the responses that differed from person to person also come together.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen the classification results, let us explain why the writing rules are included in the guidelines.

screens.title: Commentary: Why style rules are in guidelines and the topic of the day is in conversation
screens.lead: Click the Next Step button to check the reasons step by step. Just follow the flow to reach the conclusion.

steps.title: Stylistic rules are the same for everyone
steps.body: Stylistic rules should be the same for everyone and in every conversation. If you write them down in one place, the answers that vary from person to person will come together. Even if one person omits a rule, the result does not change. Newly joined team members can also use the same assistant without having to learn the rules separately.

steps.title: The product follows the instructions
steps.body: In ChatGPT projects, project guidelines take precedence over global custom guidelines. So your business style doesn't have to worry about your personal preferences. If you choose the right place for a rule, the product will apply that rule consistently. Conversely, if you pick the wrong spot, your personal settings may override the rules.

steps.title: If you write today's topic in the instructions,
steps.body: If you write down today's topic in the instructions, you will avoid the error of trying to answer with the same topic in tomorrow's conversation. This is because the guidelines are automatically applied to all conversations. Any information that changes should be addressed in conversation, not as guidance. Modifying the instructions will affect the response of all users, so it is not suitable for daily changes.

steps.title: Chat doesn't remember each other
steps.body: The Claude Project does not automatically share context between chats. Rules spoken in one chat will not be followed in another, so you should always put the rules you need in your guidelines or project knowledge.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: What does not change is left in the guidelines, and what does change is left in the conversation. Guidelines are the basis that the assistant must always follow, and instructions during conversation are the request of the day. Teams with this distinction receive the same quality of answers from the same assistant.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the reasons, let us summarize the main points of the lesson.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Let's summarize the contents of this class one more time. Read below and answer the first question.

paragraphs: The first question was which rules should be written down once and which rules should be said every time. The answer lies in the nature of the rules. Rules that apply to all conversations and that do not change for a long time are written down once in the instructions. Conditions that apply only to today's work or that change frequently are mentioned as instructions during conversation.

When making a decision, we ask three questions: repeatability, scope, and stability. Are you saying the same thing every time, every conversation, or does it not change for months? The more it fits all three, the more likely it is to be a candidate for guidance.

Although ChatGPT's project, GPT, Claude's project, and Gemini's Gem have different names, they are structured with a separate section for writing instructions and uploading data. No matter which product you use, you can set the rules based on the same criteria.

Finally, think back to the first scene. The reason why Ga-eun, Do-yoon, and Seo-yeon received different answers was because the writing rules were not gathered in one place. By writing down the rules in instructions and only asking for the day to be mentioned in conversation, all three people get the same questions and answers in the same format. The key to this class is to change from a method where a person remembers and guesses something to a method where the settings match it.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Writing too much in the instructions doesn't mean it's good. Write down only repetitive and stable rules briefly, and leave today's requests to the conversation.

glossary.def: These are rules that you write down once in your Assistant settings and apply to all conversations with that Assistant. These include project instructions, GPT Instructions, and Gem instructions.
A request entered within a conversation window and has effect only within that conversation.
The rule is reapplied even if you open a new conversation. Instructions are continuous and there are no directives during the conversation.
This is the unit of influence of the rule. Instructions apply to an entire project or GPT, and instructions during a conversation apply to a single conversation.

misconceptions.myth: The more you write in the instructions, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Only repeat and stable rules are included in the instructions. If you write down changing requests, such as today's topic or this week's deadline, in the guidelines, they will follow the conversation on other days as well.

misconceptions.myth: Once you say something in a conversation, you remember it in other conversations as well.
misconceptions.fact: According to the Claude project instructions, context is not automatically shared between chats within the project. Always place what you need in your instructions or project knowledge.

misconceptions.myth: Project guidelines and personal global guidelines are applied jointly without distinction.
misconceptions.fact: ChatGPT help explains that project guidelines apply only within that project and take precedence over global custom guidelines.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Guidelines are a set of rules that apply to every conversation.
Directions during a conversation are requests of the day that are effective only within that conversation.
Repeatability, coverage, and reliability determine what rules to include in instructions and what to say in conversations.
Although the names of Project, GPT, and Gem are different, they are structured with separate instructions and knowledge sections.

checks.q: We have a team that runs sales report assistants. Which of the following would be most appropriate to note in system-level instructions?
options: Today's topic is a review of Company A's meeting.
The rule is that all reports should be written in formal language and summarized in three lines.
Deadline to report by this Friday
Name of the customer for this request
checks.explain: Guidelines are automatically applied to all of your Assistant's conversations, so they're the place to go for writing conventions that are repeated and don't change for a long time.

wrong.0: Today's topic changes from conversation to conversation, so leave it as an instruction during the conversation.
wrong.2: Since the date is subject to change, if you write it down in the instructions, the same deadline will follow next week.
wrong.3: Since the information changes depending on the request, it is better to mention it in conversation.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match the criteria that determine whether to include in the guidelines or the conversation with the questions that the criteria raises.
right: Is this a rule that won't change for months?
Are you repeating the same thing every time?
Does this apply to all conversations or just today?
checks.explain: The question of repeatability is whether the words are repeated every time, whether they apply to all conversations is a question of scope, and whether they do not change for a long time is a question of stability. The more all three criteria are met, the more likely a guideline candidate is.
